name: Adapting models across domains
gist: Time series models trained on one source (e.g., one hospital or factory) often fail elsewhere. Papers tackle domain adaptation, generalization, and alignment to new environments.
explain: A model trained on one hospital's patient data often fails on another hospital's data, even if they treat the same diseases. A model trained on one factory's equipment fails on similar equipment at another factory. A model trained on historical weather patterns for 2020 fails in 2024 because the climate has shifted. This is domain adaptation or distribution shift. The core issue is that the input sequences in the new domain are different from training data in systematic ways. The hospital might use different sensors. The factory might have different ambient conditions. The weather patterns have changed due to climate. If you retrain from scratch, you can handle these shifts, but retraining is expensive and requires lots of labeled data in the new domain.

The challenge is knowing what is truly invariant versus what is domain-specific. In healthcare, the biological principles of disease are invariant, but sensor calibration and patient demographics are domain-specific. In manufacturing, the physics of wear is invariant, but equipment models and operating conditions are domain-specific. A smart transfer approach learns the invariant part—say, how disease progresses—and adapts the domain-specific part—sensor offsets or population statistics. The harder case is when the domain shift is subtle. If a hospital's patient population becomes older, or more obese, or sicker, the distribution of vital signs changes in ways that are hard to characterize and adapt to without labeled data.

Papers in this cluster tackle alignment and adaptation. Some use domain adversarial training, which forces the model to learn representations that are useful for prediction but invariant to domain identity. Others use meta-learning: learn to learn in a way that transfers well. Some use unsupervised adaptation, where the model observes unlabeled sequences in the new domain and tunes itself to fit without ground truth. A few use causal models, assuming that the causal structure of a sequence is invariant even if the model's internal weights shift, and then adapt those weights. The underlying insight is that data in the wild is nonstationary—it drifts over time and across contexts—so models that can adapt are more valuable than models that are frozen.

papers.title: PATRA: Pattern-Aware Alignment and Balanced Reasoning for Time Series Question Answering
papers.contribution: Outperforms baselines on diverse Time Series Question Answering tasks; demonstrates superior cross-modal understanding and reasoning capability.

papers.title: Rating Quality of Diverse Time Series Data by Meta-learning from LLM Judgment
papers.contribution: Ensures cross-domain adaptability while improving training efficiency, validated on eleven benchmarks across three time series tasks.

papers.title: Winformer: Transcending Pairwise Similarity for Time-series Generation
papers.contribution: Winformer achieves an average performance gain of 10.67% over SOTA baselines on 12 real-world time-series generation datasets.
